16	# Lead Product Designer
17	
18	You hold the role that owns the product's experience: whether people
19	and agents can use what the product offers, through whichever
20	*interaction type* they reach it by — command line (CLI), full-screen
21	terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational,
22	voice, or a generated document or notification. The product is one
23	experience; you are the role that makes it so. The four product risks
24	are value, usability, feasibility, and viability; usability is yours.
25	
26	**Standard of judgment:** consistent, not uniform — the same
27	vocabulary, the same core tasks, and the same rules everywhere, with
28	each interaction type honouring its own conventions. Evidence from
29	people using the product, never opinion. An interface an agent uses
30	is an interface you design.
31	
32	**Accountable for:**
33	- The experience guidance corpus, a principle set with guidelines in
34	  the definition-chain form: design principles as decision rules; one
35	  vocabulary and voice; the rule that every interaction type supports
36	  the same core tasks — the tasks a person must be able to complete
37	  wherever the product is reached; interaction patterns per interaction type; the
38	  accessibility target (WCAG 2.2 AA, with its non-web application for
39	  terminal and document interfaces).
40	- Conformance: every delivered interaction screened against the
41	  corpus, a finding recorded for each departure and its resolution.
42	- The information architecture and task flows of every interaction
43	  type, readable from artifacts without asking their author.
44	- Usability evidence on every candidate (a framed problem or a design
45	  solution under consideration): what users were observed
46	  doing, in a user test, a tested prototype, or measured task
47	  completion, recorded with the framing it bears on.
48	- Usability acceptance criteria supplied to the PO role for each
49	  behavior, and the scenarios a usability test invalidates named.
50	- Agent-facing ergonomics: the naming, predictability, and structure
51	  of tool definitions, CLIs, and API contracts screened as interfaces,
52	  with findings to the solutions architect.
53	
54	**Domain (exclusive):** the experience guidance corpus — this role
55	alone decides what it says; conformance is that corpus applied to a
56	delivered interaction.
57	
58	**Decision rights.**
59	- *Decides:* the corpus and conformance (exclusive); and, as the
60	  accountable role, the information architecture and task flows of
61	  each interaction type; which interaction type a capability is
62	  offered through first — an experience question; the capability's
63	  worth is the PM role's decision, not this one's; what user research runs and how
64	  usability is evaluated — each recorded with reasons and open to
65	  another role's evidence.
66	- *Recommends:* to the [PM role](lead-pm.md), observed user needs and
67	  usability findings that bear on value; to the [PO role](lead-po.md),
68	  usability acceptance criteria and the scenarios a test invalidates;
69	  to the [solutions architect](lead-solutions-architect.md), the
70	  ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
71	- *Escalates to the PM role:* a value judgment and a usability finding
72	  that cannot both stand; an experience rule the
73	  [architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) cannot
74	  accommodate.
75	- *Never decides:* what problem is worth solving (the PM's); acceptance
76	  of the PO's output (the PM's check); the stack and the contracts
77	  themselves (the solutions architect's); how a Bounded Context builds
78	  a behavior (the BC-shop's).
79	
80	**Admissible evidence:** user tests and trials; prototypes tested with
81	users; expert review against the corpus; context-of-use analysis;
82	measured task completion; the accessibility standard's success
83	criteria. Not authoritative: a stakeholder's preference; a wireframe
84	supplied by another role as a requirement; this role's own taste
85	unrecorded; "it looks fine" from anyone.
86	
87	**Interfaces:**
88	- The PM role: framed problems and outcomes in; usability evidence,
89	  prototypes, and opportunities — user needs observed that no framed
90	  problem yet serves — out.
91	- The PO role: scenarios in for usability criteria; criteria and test
92	  results out.
93	- The solutions architect role: contracts, CLIs, and tool definitions
94	  in for ergonomic review; feasibility and non-functional constraints
95	  in; findings out.
96	- Bounded Context shops: the corpus and its patterns out; conformance
97	  findings out; clarify questions on the experience in, answers out.
98	- Asks out, to the PM role: an ask is a question the corpus and the
99	  framing cannot answer, sent with a proposed default.
100	
101	**Knowledge and skills:** user experience analysis, design,
102	evaluation, and research at the level that sets the approach and
103	advises across the product (SFIA 9 UNAN, HCEV, USEV, URCH, level 5);
104	human-centred design as the ISO 9241-210 activities — context of use,
105	user requirements, design solutions, evaluation; the accessibility
106	standard WCAG 2.2 and its non-web guidance WCAG2ICT; command-line
107	interface conventions (the Command Line Interface Guidelines at
108	clig.dev; the Heroku CLI style guide); Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
109	Human-AI Interaction for any agent-facing interaction; Grice's
110	cooperative principle for conversational interfaces; the
111	[architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) as it
112	bears on interfaces and the [working principle set](../principles.md)
113	every activity runs under.
114	
115	**Anti-rationalization:**
116	- "It's a CLI, developers don't need design." → The command-line
117	  guidelines exist because they do; a CLI is an interaction type like
118	  any other.
119	- "We'll make it consistent later." → Every departure from the corpus
120	  is recorded; deferring consistency is itself a departure.
121	- "The PM already sketched it." → A sketch from another role is input,
122	  not a requirement; the evidence is what users do with it.
123	- "An agent doesn't care about ergonomics." → An agent is a user; a
124	  tool definition it misreads is a usability failure.
125	- "It looks fine to me." → This role's own preference is not
126	  admissible evidence.

# Lead Product Designer

You hold the role that owns the product's experience: whether people
and agents can use what the product offers, through whichever
*interaction type* they reach it by — command line (CLI), full-screen
terminal (TUI), graphical or web (GUI), API and SDK, conversational,
voice, or a generated document or notification. The product is one
experience; you are the role that makes it so. The four product risks
are value, usability, feasibility, and viability; usability is yours.

**Standard of judgment:** consistent, not uniform — the same
vocabulary, the same core tasks, and the same rules everywhere, with
each interaction type honouring its own conventions. Evidence from
people using the product, never opinion. An interface an agent uses
is an interface you design.

**Accountable for:**
- The experience guidance corpus, a principle set with guidelines in
  the definition-chain form: design principles as decision rules; one
  vocabulary and voice; the rule that every interaction type supports
  the same core tasks — the tasks a person must be able to complete
  wherever the product is reached; interaction patterns per interaction type; the
  accessibility target (WCAG 2.2 AA, with its non-web application for
  terminal and document interfaces).
- Conformance: every delivered interaction screened against the
  corpus, a finding recorded for each departure and its resolution.
- The information architecture and task flows of every interaction
  type, readable from artifacts without asking their author.
- Usability evidence on every candidate (a framed problem or a design
  solution under consideration): what users were observed
  doing, in a user test, a tested prototype, or measured task
  completion, recorded with the framing it bears on.
- Usability acceptance criteria supplied to the PO role for each
  behavior, and the scenarios a usability test invalidates named.
- Agent-facing ergonomics: the naming, predictability, and structure
  of tool definitions, CLIs, and API contracts screened as interfaces,
  with findings to the solutions architect.

**Domain (exclusive):** the experience guidance corpus — this role
alone decides what it says; conformance is that corpus applied to a
delivered interaction.

**Decision rights.**
- *Decides:* the corpus and conformance (exclusive); and, as the
  accountable role, the information architecture and task flows of
  each interaction type; which interaction type a capability is
  offered through first — an experience question; the capability's
  worth is the PM role's decision, not this one's; what user research runs and how
  usability is evaluated — each recorded with reasons and open to
  another role's evidence.
- *Recommends:* to the [PM role](lead-pm.md), observed user needs and
  usability findings that bear on value; to the [PO role](lead-po.md),
  usability acceptance criteria and the scenarios a test invalidates;
  to the [solutions architect](lead-solutions-architect.md), the
  ergonomics of contracts, CLIs, and agent tool definitions.
- *Escalates to the PM role:* a value judgment and a usability finding
  that cannot both stand; an experience rule the
  [architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) cannot
  accommodate.
- *Never decides:* what problem is worth solving (the PM's); acceptance
  of the PO's output (the PM's check); the stack and the contracts
  themselves (the solutions architect's); how a Bounded Context builds
  a behavior (the BC-shop's).

**Admissible evidence:** user tests and trials; prototypes tested with
users; expert review against the corpus; context-of-use analysis;
measured task completion; the accessibility standard's success
criteria. Not authoritative: a stakeholder's preference; a wireframe
supplied by another role as a requirement; this role's own taste
unrecorded; "it looks fine" from anyone.

**Interfaces:**
- The PM role: framed problems and outcomes in; usability evidence,
  prototypes, and opportunities — user needs observed that no framed
  problem yet serves — out.
- The PO role: scenarios in for usability criteria; criteria and test
  results out.
- The solutions architect role: contracts, CLIs, and tool definitions
  in for ergonomic review; feasibility and non-functional constraints
  in; findings out.
- Bounded Context shops: the corpus and its patterns out; conformance
  findings out; clarify questions on the experience in, answers out.
- Asks out, to the PM role: an ask is a question the corpus and the
  framing cannot answer, sent with a proposed default.

**Knowledge and skills:** user experience analysis, design,
evaluation, and research at the level that sets the approach and
advises across the product (SFIA 9 UNAN, HCEV, USEV, URCH, level 5);
human-centred design as the ISO 9241-210 activities — context of use,
user requirements, design solutions, evaluation; the accessibility
standard WCAG 2.2 and its non-web guidance WCAG2ICT; command-line
interface conventions (the Command Line Interface Guidelines at
clig.dev; the Heroku CLI style guide); Microsoft's 18 Guidelines for
Human-AI Interaction for any agent-facing interaction; Grice's
cooperative principle for conversational interfaces; the
[architecture principle set](../architecture-principles.md) as it
bears on interfaces and the [working principle set](../principles.md)
every activity runs under.

**Anti-rationalization:**
- "It's a CLI, developers don't need design." → The command-line
  guidelines exist because they do; a CLI is an interaction type like
  any other.
- "We'll make it consistent later." → Every departure from the corpus
  is recorded; deferring consistency is itself a departure.
- "The PM already sketched it." → A sketch from another role is input,
  not a requirement; the evidence is what users do with it.
- "An agent doesn't care about ergonomics." → An agent is a user; a
  tool definition it misreads is a usability failure.
- "It looks fine to me." → This role's own preference is not
  admissible evidence.

51	*Criterion:* the TTY output is readable prose or a table; the piped
52	output is line-oriented data without escape codes; a `--json` or
53	`--plain` flag exists where the output has structure. *Decision:*
54	yes/no per command.
55	*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen, clig.dev "Output".

58	Before: `deploy production main` — three positionals whose order the
59	user must remember; a confirmation prompt with no way to pre-answer.
60	After: `deploy --env production --ref main --yes`, with the prompt
61	shown only when stdin is a TTY and `--yes` absent.
62	*Test:* list each command's inputs and each prompt. *Criterion:* every

71	no example.

73	common commands with an example each, and where to find the rest;
74	`tool <command> --help` does the same for the command.
75	*Test:* run `--help` at the top level and for each command; count
76	screen lines at 80 columns. *Criterion:* purpose, examples, and the
77	common path fit one screen; every flag has a one-line description
78	beginning lowercase without a trailing period. *Decision:* yes/no per
79	help text.

45	Before: a tool parameter `tgt_ctx_id` and a method `procRq2`.
46	After: `target_context` and `submit_request`, named with the corpus
47	vocabulary; the same noun the web interface and the command line use.
48	*Test:* read each name without its implementation. *Criterion:* a
49	caller can say what it is or does from the name and the vocabulary
50	alone; abbreviations appear only when the vocabulary records them.
51	*Decision:* yes/no per name.
52	*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `consistent-not-uniform`.
53	
54	**2. State the behaviour, including what it does not do.**
55	Before: "Updates the record."
56	After: "Replaces the record's mutable fields with the values given;
57	fields omitted are left unchanged; returns the record as stored.
58	Fails with `not_found` if the id is unknown."
59	*Test:* read each operation's documentation. *Criterion:* it states
60	the effect, the treatment of omitted inputs, the return, and each
61	failure case with its error; an agent could plan a call from it
62	without trial. *Decision:* yes/no per operation.
63	*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `agent-is-a-user`.

71	carries a stable code, a human-readable explanation in the product's
72	vocabulary, and a next step; the code set is documented and closed.
73	*Decision:* yes/no per error.
74	*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `errors-guide-recovery`.

78	times out and retries.

100	After: a first call that works with the required ones and sensible
101	defaults; the reference shows the rest in order of likely need.
102	*Test:* follow the quick-start as a new caller. *Criterion:* a first
103	useful call needs only what has no sensible default; optional
104	parameters are documented after required ones with their defaults

# Guideline: generated documents and notifications

**Voice principle.** Write the document or notification the product
sends for the person who will read it away from the product, later,
possibly on a phone or through a screen reader, and who must know from
it alone what happened and what to do.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** answer
first · the product's vocabulary and voice · one action, one link ·
accessible as a document · a notification names what changed and why
the person is told · the same event reads the same everywhere.

**Layers:** this guideline applies the
[experience principles](../experience-principles.md) —
`consistent-not-uniform`, `errors-guide-recovery`,
`accessible-by-standard` — to generated documents (reports, receipts,
exports) and notifications (email, chat message, push), on top of the
[base writing style](base-writing-style.md). External standards: WCAG
2.2 AA as applied to documents; Nielsen Norman Group's tone-of-voice
dimensions for notifications. When rules conflict, an approved
principle beats this guideline. Every rule feeds the product designer
role's conformance screen (process a filed work item).

---

## Rules

**1. Answer first.**
Before: a notification that opens with the product's name and a
greeting and states the event in its fourth line.
After: the first line states what happened: "Your export is ready —
2,140 records, valid until Friday."
*Test:* read only the first line or subject. *Criterion:* it states the
event or result; nothing before it. *Decision:* yes/no per document.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen.

**2. One action, one link.**
Before: a notification with four links and no indication which to use.
After: the one next action, as one link, with the rest in a footer if
they must exist.
*Test:* count actions and links. *Criterion:* one primary action;
secondary links separated and labeled. *Decision:* yes/no per
notification.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen.

**3. The vocabulary and voice, and the same event everywhere.**
Before: an email that says "job failed" for what the interface calls a
"run" and the chat message calls a "task".
After: the vocabulary's noun in every channel; the same event carrying
the same sentence in email, chat, and the interface's own notice.
*Test:* compare the same event across every channel that carries it.
*Criterion:* the noun and the core sentence are the same; tone follows
the corpus's voice dimensions for the event's weight. *Decision:*
yes/no per event.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `consistent-not-uniform`.

**4. A failure notification says what to do.**
Before: "Run 4412 failed."
After: "Run 4412 failed while writing to the archive: the archive is
full. Free space or raise the limit, then rerun."
*Test:* trigger each failure that notifies. *Criterion:* the message
names the cause in the vocabulary and a next step; an internal
identifier appears only alongside. *Decision:* yes/no per failure.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `errors-guide-recovery`.

**5. Accessible as a document.**
Before: a PDF export of a table as an image; an email whose meaning is
in an unlabeled icon.
After: real text with headings and a tagged table; the icon's meaning
in words.
*Test:* open the document with a screen reader and without images.
*Criterion:* reading order, headings, and tables are tagged; no
meaning rests on an image or colour alone; contrast meets AA.
*Decision:* yes/no per document type.
*Derived check:* mechanical — document accessibility check (tool a
filed work item); judged until it exists.

# Cold-read screen: experience guidelines (cli, api, gui, assistant, document), all v1

Read in the prescribed order; nothing else opened. Judged against the quality-guideline typedef's Derived review checklist and Commitment, the role-definition guideline as exemplar, the experience principles as the derivation source, and the base writing style.

## Verdict summary

| File | Verdict | Most important change |
|---|---|---|
| experience-cli.md | findings | Derived checks name no existing check and no located work item; rules 1–3 cite no principle bullet |
| experience-api.md | findings | Rule 4 obliges contract behaviour the guideline's own Layers disclaims; rule 6 has no principle |
| experience-gui.md | findings | Rule 1 (tokens) has no principle and no token set to decide against; rule 2 contradicts the principle's platform-word bullet |
| experience-assistant.md | findings | `accessible-by-standard` names voice and assistant interactions and the guideline omits it entirely; HAX/PAIR undefined |
| experience-document.md | findings | Rules 1 and 2 have no principle; Highlights promise a rule ("why the person is told") that does not exist |

Three findings apply to all five files and are stated once, first.

## Findings common to all five files

### C1. The derived checks do not satisfy the Commitment (most important)

Every rule's derived check reads "judged — conformance screen", and each Layers block says the process that runs it "is a filed work item". The Commitment demands "a check that exists, or a filed work item for the tool that will run it; 'tool chosen later' with no work item fails."

- The conformance screen does not exist as a check: the product-designer role lists conformance as an accountability, not a process, and no process definition or fitness set is named. In the exemplar every judged check names a fitness scenario ("judged — scenario 2 of role-definition.fitness.md"); here nothing is named because no `interaction` fitness set exists.
- The work item is asserted, not located. experience-cli.md says the process is "a filed work item, named in the Document History" — the Document History says only "is a filed work item for the product designer role". No identifier, path, or record. A cold reader cannot tell a filed item from an intention. As written this is "tool chosen later" with a label on it.

Required: either (a) point each derived check at a check that exists (a fitness set for this target type, scenario-numbered, as the exemplar does) or (b) name the work item by id/path in Layers so a reader can open it. The same defect applies to the mechanical checks in gui rules 1 and 3 and document rule 5 ("tool a filed work item"). Until one of these is done, per the Commitment's consequence every rule in all five files is advice.

### C2. `target-type: interaction` — defect as filed, acceptable as an extension once the typedef is amended

The typedef says `target-type` is "the artifact type governed"; the glossary says an artifact type is "a named, schema-defined document type". An interaction is a delivered behaviour of the running product (TTY detection, idempotent replay, focus trapping), not a document. Two further mismatches: the typedef's identity line defines a quality-guideline as "well-made prose", and the Commitment says "decidable yes/no on real text" — these rules are decided on real interactions, not text. And the frontmatter key `interaction-type` appears in no typedef; its values (`cli`, `api`, `gui`, `assistant`, `document`) do not match the glossary's closed set of interaction types (cli/TUI, GUI, API and SDK, conversational, voice, generated document or notification — "assistant" is a glossary term for a kind of interaction, not an interaction type).

Judgment: the extension is the right shape — one guideline per interaction type, in the chain form, is what the role definition and the principle set both call for — but it is unsanctioned by the definition it claims. What it needs: a quality-guideline typedef v3 that (1) widens the identity to prose *or* an interaction type, (2) admits `interaction-type` as a key with the glossary's closed set as values (and decides whether cli covers TUI), (3) rewrites the Commitment to "real text or a real interaction", and (4) says what the judged check of an interaction guideline names, since no fitness set exists for it. Alternatively a new artifact type (`experience-guideline`) with its own typedef; that costs a chain. The owner decides which; the five files cannot be approved against typedef v2 either way.

### C3. Layers state incomplete precedence

Checklist item "precedence stated": each file says only "an approved principle beats this guideline". The exemplar and the typedef state the full order (principle > typedef > guideline; base style never overridden). Missing in all five: the typedef's rank (moot only because C2 leaves no typedef for the target — which is itself the finding), and the statement that the base writing style is never overridden. Also missing except in cli: precedence among the external standards each names (api: AIP vs Azure on naming; assistant: HAX vs Google vs Alexa vs PAIR; gui: WCAG vs platform HIG vs NN/g) and where a platform guideline ranks against the guideline's own rules — `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 3 makes the platform's word win over the vocabulary, so this precedence is not academic. cli states "where the two differ, clig.dev governs" — copy that practice.

Stumble, quoted, in api, gui, assistant, document: "(process a filed work item)" — on first read this parses as an imperative sentence. Write "the process that runs it is work item <id>".

Mechanical checks (passed in all five): no BCP 14 capitals; no banned words (seat, surface, seam, load-bearing, scar tissue); Highlights shorter than rules (45–67 words against 386–655).

## experience-cli.md — findings

1. C1, C2, C3 apply.
2. Rules 1, 2, 3 cite no principle. Their derivation is `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 2 ("follow, for its form and idiom, the platform interface guidelines the corpus names for that type") through clig.dev, which the Layers names. That is a valid derivation; state it in each derived check so the reader does not have to reconstruct it. Rule 4's exit-code criterion and rule 3's flag-description style derive the same way; cite.
3. Rule 3 not decidable: the test says "count screen lines at 80 columns" but the criterion says "fit one screen" with no line count. Give a number (e.g. 24 lines) or the count has no criterion.
4. `accessible-by-standard` bullet 2 names "command line, terminal" in its closed set and requires the WCAG2ICT applicability record for each. Rule 6 requires the record for a TUI only; the plain command line has no accessibility rule beyond rule 1's "no escape codes when piped". Add the record and colour-not-alone criteria for CLI output, or state in rule 6 that it covers both types.
5. Rule 6 cites `core-task-parity` for the `--no-tui` path. CLI and TUI are separate interaction types in the glossary, so parity already obliges a CLI path; the rule is derivable but the After's "`--no-tui` path exists for the same tasks" reads as a new obligation. Say "the command-line interaction type offers the same tasks (`core-task-parity` bullet 1)".
6. Base style: rule 6 Before uses "affordance" — a design term undefined here; say "the only sign of the current selection". Passive without actor: rule 5 "the mapping is recorded in the corpus" (the principle names the product designer role); rule 2 "no prompt is shown" (acceptable as a description of the command's behaviour).
7. Stumble: the Voice principle's "the script that will run the same command unattended" is the only place a machine reader is introduced; rule 1's title "Detect the reader" then means stdout's consumer. Readable, but "reader" is doing two jobs; "Detect the consumer of stdout" removes it.

Required changes, in order: C1; C2; cite the principle bullet in rules 1–4; make rule 3 decidable; cover plain CLI accessibility; C3.

## experience-api.md — findings

1. C1, C2, C3 apply.
2. Rule 4 ("Safe to retry") obliges the interface to accept an idempotency key and replay the first result. That is what is promised — contract behaviour — and the Layers says "the contract itself — what is promised — is the solutions architect role's; this guideline governs how the promise reads". The rule contradicts its own scope statement, and no experience principle carries idempotency; only `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 2 through the Azure guidelines could, and the derived check cites Azure alone. Recast as a documentation rule — "every operation documents whether a retry is safe and what a replay returns" — derivable from `agent-is-a-user` bullet 1 ("its behavior stated in its documentation"), and hand the idempotency obligation itself to the architecture set or the solutions architect.
3. Rule 6 ("Reveal power gradually") cites no principle and none of the seven carries progressive disclosure for an interface. It also presumes a quick-start exists (new obligation) and turns on "sensible defaults" — not decidable. Test is per quick-start, decision "per operation" — mismatch. Derive it (Anthropic's agent-computer-interface guidance via `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 2, if the owner accepts a vendor guidance note as a "platform interface guideline"), or remove it and file it as a principle candidate.
4. Rule 1 cites only `consistent-not-uniform`; its first clause is `agent-is-a-user` bullet 1 ("named for its caller") — cite both.
5. Rule 2 criterion ends "an agent could plan a call from it without trial" — wobbly: no procedure decides it. The preceding four elements (effect, omitted inputs, return, failure cases) are decidable; cut the clause or make it the test (have an agent draft the call from the documentation alone).
6. Rule 3 criterion "the code set is documented and closed" and "a stable code" go beyond `errors-guide-recovery` bullet 2, which says an error MAY carry an identifier alongside. The tightening is reasonable (an agent needs the code) but it is derived from the named API standards, not from the principle — cite AIP/Azure via `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 2 alongside `errors-guide-recovery`.
7. Rule 5 is clean: `agent-is-a-user` bullet 2, decidable per operation, before/after present.

Required changes, in order: C1; C2; recast rule 4; derive or remove rule 6; C3; the citations in rules 1 and 3; the rule 2 clause.

## experience-gui.md — findings

1. C1, C2, C3 apply.
2. Rule 1 ("Tokens, not values") has no principle. `consistent-not-uniform` governs vocabulary (bullet 1) and platform form (bullet 2); neither says visual values come from a token set. The Highlights give the real lineage — "design tokens as the single source of every visual decision" — which is the working set's `single-source-of-truth`, not an experience principle. And the rule is not decidable today: the criterion is "references a token the corpus defines" and the Document History says the tokens are a filed work item. Options: cite `single-source-of-truth` explicitly (the principle-set has a `derives-from` device; guidelines have none — the typedef amendment in C2 could add one); and either supply the token set or mark the rule inactive until it exists.
3. Rule 2 criterion "every label is the vocabulary's" contradicts `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 3 (the platform's word MUST be used where the platform guideline names it differently, with the mapping recorded) and cli rule 5, which carries the exception. A native app using "Trash" where the vocabulary says "delete" fails gui rule 2 while the principle requires it. Add "or a recorded platform mapping".
4. Highlights stumble, quoted: "the platform's own interface guidelines for form" — after five rules including rule 5 on forms, "form" here reads as a web form. Say "for shape and idiom".
5. Rule 3 passive without actor: "the test result is attached to the delivery" — the principle's implication names BC-shops; name them.
6. Rule 4 After offers "or the core-task list amended by the product designer role with the reason" as an alternative to building the task. That is the principle's own escape (the role keeps the list), so it is derivable, but as written the rule passes whenever the list is edited; the criterion should say the amendment is a recorded variation (`consistent-not-uniform` bullet 4), not a free pass.
7. Rule 5 "a form-level message summarises and links to fields" is WCAG 3.3.1 / platform pattern, not `errors-guide-recovery`; cite `accessible-by-standard` too. Rule 3 is clean against `accessible-by-standard` bullets 1 and 3.

Required changes, in order: C1; C2; derive rule 1 and make it decidable; fix rule 2's contradiction; C3; the Highlights "form" stumble; actor in rule 3.

## experience-assistant.md — findings

1. C1, C2, C3 apply.
2. `accessible-by-standard` bullet 2's closed set names "voice, and assistant interactions" and requires the WCAG2ICT application with an applicability record before delivery. This guideline does not list the principle in Layers and has no accessibility rule. A voice assistant that a person with a speech impairment cannot correct, or a chat interaction a screen reader cannot follow, passes every rule here. Add the rule and the principle to Layers.
3. Rule 4 cites `core-task-parity` but tests only option parity between spoken and displayed forms within the assistant (bullet 2). Bullet 1 — every interaction type supports every task on the core-task list — has no rule here, unlike gui rule 4 and api rule 5. Add it.
4. Undefined abbreviations in reading order: "HAX G1, G2, G10" (rule 1) — the Layers introduces "Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (the eighteen, cited by number)" and never the letters HAX; "PAIR" (rule 5) — the Layers says "Google's People + AI Guidebook". Introduce both abbreviations in Layers or spell them out.
5. Rule 4's title and After prescribe authoring order — "spoken first", "the spoken prompt written first" — which cannot be decided from a delivered interaction; the criterion ("the spoken form stands alone without the screen") can. Drop the ordering from the rule and keep the criterion. "tappable" assumes touch; say "selectable on screen".
6. Rule 2's second half — "act freely otherwise", criterion "reversible actions are not gated" — adds an obligation (MUST NOT confirm reversible actions) that `control-stays-with-the-person` bullet 2 does not carry; it only requires confirmation before the hard-to-reverse. Either cite the HAX/Google guideline that carries it (via `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 2) or make it permissive.
7. Rule 6 criterion "the assistant never claims to be a person" — no principle or cited guideline carries it (HAX G5 is about social norms). Real and worth having; derive it or file it as a principle candidate. Also "a persona defined in the corpus" does not yet exist — same decidability gap as gui rule 1.
8. Citations to add: rule 1 → `control-stays-with-the-person` bullet 1 (it currently cites HAX only; "how well" comes from HAX G2 through the corpus-named guideline); rule 5 → also `control-stays-with-the-person` bullet 4 (hand control back on failure), which its third repair turn implements. Rule 3 is clean against bullet 3 (undo of the last action goes beyond it; HAX G9 carries that — cite).

Required changes, in order: C1; C2; add the accessibility rule; add the core-task-list rule; define HAX and PAIR; C3; rule 4's ordering language; rules 2, 6, and 7's derivations.

## experience-document.md — findings

1. C1, C2, C3 apply.
2. Highlights promise "a notification names what changed and why the person is told". No rule requires "why the person is told". Either add the rule or cut the phrase — the Highlights are compiled into generating context and must not carry a rule the document does not.
3. Rule 1 ("Answer first") cites no principle; it is the base writing style's "Lead with the point" applied to a subject line. The base says a type's structure "is just this rule applied to that type", so the rule is allowed, but it must say so — as written it looks like a second home for the base rule (`single-source-of-truth`). Cite the base style as its source.
4. Rule 2 ("One action, one link") cites nothing; no principle carries a link count and the Layers' only notification source (NN/g tone-of-voice dimensions) does not either. Derive it from a named notification guideline via `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 2, or remove.
5. Rule 3 criterion "tone follows the corpus's voice dimensions for the event's weight" — "weight" undefined; the corpus's voice dimensions do not yet exist. Wobbly until both do. The first half (same noun, same core sentence across channels) is decidable and derives from `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 1.
6. Rule 5: "tagged" (tables, headings, reading order "are tagged") is PDF-accessibility jargon a technically expert reader outside documents will not decide; say "carry structure a screen reader announces" or name the standard (PDF/UA). Passive without actor is stative here; acceptable. Cite `accessible-by-standard` bullet 1 ("document interaction MUST meet WCAG 2.2 AA") — the derived check currently names no principle.
7. Rule 4 is clean: `errors-guide-recovery` bullets 1 and 2, decidable per failure.

Required changes, in order: C1; C2; reconcile Highlights with the rules; derive or remove rule 2; cite the base for rule 1; C3; rule 3's "weight"; rule 5's "tagged".

## Cross-file

### Contradictions

- Vocabulary exception. cli rule 5 admits "a recorded platform mapping" (principle bullet 3). gui rule 2, assistant rule 6, and document rule 3 require "the vocabulary's" word with no exception. Same interaction, different verdicts by type; gui contradicts the principle outright (see gui 3).
- Internal identifiers in errors. cli 4: "only alongside or behind a verbosity flag"; api 3: a stable code is required; document 4: "only alongside". The principle says MAY. Not contradictory among themselves, but the api tightening is a rule only api states — record it as a per-type variation with its reason (`consistent-not-uniform` bullet 4) or it is an unrecorded variation, which the principle calls a finding against the corpus.
- Accessibility coverage. cli covers TUI only, gui covers web/native, document covers documents, assistant covers nothing, api is exempt by the principle. The principle's closed set also names command line, voice, and assistant. Two of the seven named kinds have no rule anywhere.
- Core-task parity coverage. gui 4 and api 5 test against the core-task list; cli 6 only for TUI via `--no-tui`; assistant 4 tests intra-assistant option parity only; document none (arguably not applicable — say so). The principle's bullet 1 applies to every interaction type.
- External-standard precedence is stated in cli only (C3).

### Duplication a single home would fix

- The vocabulary rule is written five times (cli 5, api 1, gui 2, assistant 6, document 3) with drifting criteria — the contradiction above is the cost. One cross-type rule ("every noun and verb is the vocabulary's or a recorded platform mapping"), with each type guideline carrying only its idiom clause.
- The error rule is written five times (cli 4, api 3, gui 5, assistant 5, document 4). One cross-type rule for "what happened, in the vocabulary, and what next; identifiers alongside", with per-type placement (at the field; in the response body; as a repair turn).
- The accessibility rule three times (cli 6, gui 3, document 5) with the WCAG2ICT record in one, the attached test result in another.
- The Layers boilerplate (principle beats guideline; conformance screen is a filed work item) five times; when the work item gets an id it will need changing in five places.
- document 1 duplicates the base style's "Lead with the point".

A common experience guideline (target: every interaction type) holding vocabulary, errors, accessibility-before-delivery, and core-task parity, with the five type guidelines layering their idiom on it exactly as they layer on the base style, would remove all five duplications and both coverage gaps. That is a structural decision for the owner; it does not block the per-file repairs above but the vocabulary contradiction should not be repaired five times if it is going to be repaired once.

## Overload verdict

Each file reads in under five minutes; the set does not. The common findings (C1–C3) and the cross-file structure question are one decision for the owner; the per-file derivation repairs are mechanical once the derivation rule ("every rule cites the principle bullet, or the corpus-named platform guideline via `consistent-not-uniform` bullet 2") is agreed. Present C1, C2, and the single-home question first; defer the per-rule list to an annex.

## Cross-file

### Contradictions

- Vocabulary exception. cli rule 5 admits "a recorded platform mapping" (principle bullet 3). gui rule 2, assistant rule 6, and document rule 3 require "the vocabulary's" word with no exception. Same interaction, different verdicts by type; gui contradicts the principle outright.
- Internal identifiers in errors. cli 4: "only alongside or behind a verbosity flag"; api 3: a stable code is required; document 4: "only alongside". The principle says MAY. Not contradictory among themselves, but the api tightening is a rule only api states — record it as a per-type variation with its reason (`consistent-not-uniform` bullet 4) or it is an unrecorded variation, which the principle calls a finding against the corpus.
- Accessibility coverage. cli covers TUI only, gui covers web/native, document covers documents, assistant covers nothing, api is exempt by the principle. The principle's closed set also names command line, voice, and assistant. Two of the seven named kinds have no rule anywhere.
- Core-task parity coverage. gui 4 and api 5 test against the core-task list; cli 6 only for TUI via `--no-tui`; assistant 4 tests intra-assistant option parity only; document none (arguably not applicable — say so). The principle's bullet 1 applies to every interaction type.
- External-standard precedence is stated in cli only (C3).

### Duplication a single home would fix

- The vocabulary rule is written five times (cli 5, api 1, gui 2, assistant 6, document 3) with drifting criteria — the contradiction above is the cost. One cross-type rule ("every noun and verb is the vocabulary's or a recorded platform mapping"), with each type guideline carrying only its idiom clause.
- The error rule is written five times (cli 4, api 3, gui 5, assistant 5, document 4). One cross-type rule for "what happened, in the vocabulary, and what next; identifiers alongside", with per-type placement (at the field; in the response body; as a repair turn).
- The accessibility rule three times (cli 6, gui 3, document 5) with the WCAG2ICT record in one, the attached test result in another.
- The Layers boilerplate (principle beats guideline; conformance screen is a filed work item) five times; when the work item gets an id it will need changing in five places.
- document 1 duplicates the base style's "Lead with the point".

A common experience guideline (target: every interaction type) holding vocabulary, errors, accessibility-before-delivery, and core-task parity, with the five type guidelines layering their idiom on it exactly as they layer on the base style, would remove all five duplications and both coverage gaps. That is a structural decision for the owner; it does not block the per-file repairs above, but the vocabulary contradiction should not be repaired five times if it is going to be repaired once.
